The Jacobian as a Grid Deformation

Push a rectangular grid through a map and the straight lines bend, the cells fan out.

Follow one green cell on both sides. Measure its area after the map and divide by the original area. That ratio is exactly the determinant at that spot.

For example, redraw a 🗺️ map in another projection. The same piece of land changes size on paper. The position-dependent factor is the Jacobian.

det⁡JF(a,b)=∂(x,y)∂(a,b),image area≈∣det⁡JF∣×domain area\det J_F(a, b) = \frac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (a, b)}, \qquad \text{image area} \approx |\det J_F| \times \text{domain area}detJF​(a,b)=∂(a,b)∂(x,y)​,image area≈∣detJF​∣×domain area
(r,θ)↦(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ):det⁡J=r(r, \theta) \mapsto (r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta): \quad \det J = r(r,θ)↦(rcosθ,rsinθ):detJ=r

Examples & Exercises

Find the Jacobian matrix and determinant of the polar map (r,θ)↦(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)(r, \theta) \mapsto (r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta)(r,θ)↦(rcosθ,rsinθ).

J=(cos⁡θ−rsin⁡θsin⁡θrcos⁡θ),det⁡J=rcos⁡2θ+rsin⁡2θ=rJ = \begin{pmatrix} \cos\theta & -r\sin\theta \\ \sin\theta & r\cos\theta \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \det J = r\cos^2\theta + r\sin^2\theta = rJ=(cosθsinθ​−rsinθrcosθ​),detJ=rcos2θ+rsin2θ=r
Show proof

  1. The partials are ∂x∂r=cos⁡θ\frac{\partial x}{\partial r} = \cos\theta∂r∂x​=cosθ, ∂x∂θ=−rsin⁡θ\frac{\partial x}{\partial \theta} = -r\sin\theta∂θ∂x​=−rsinθ, ∂y∂r=sin⁡θ\frac{\partial y}{\partial r} = \sin\theta∂r∂y​=sinθ, ∂y∂θ=rcos⁡θ\frac{\partial y}{\partial \theta} = r\cos\theta∂θ∂y​=rcosθ.

  2. The determinant is rcos⁡2θ+rsin⁡2θ=rr\cos^2\theta + r\sin^2\theta = rrcos2θ+rsin2θ=r: independent of the angle, proportional to the radius alone.

image areadomain area=12(2.42−1.82) Δθ0.6 Δθ=1.8+2.42=2.1\frac{\text{image area}}{\text{domain area}} = \frac{\frac12 (2.4^2 - 1.8^2)\,\Delta\theta}{0.6\,\Delta\theta} = \frac{1.8 + 2.4}{2} = 2.1domain areaimage area​=0.6Δθ21​(2.42−1.82)Δθ​=21.8+2.4​=2.1
Show proof

  1. An annular sector has area 12(r22−r12) Δθ\frac12 (r_2^2 - r_1^2)\,\Delta\theta21​(r22​−r12​)Δθ, and the domain cell has area (r2−r1) Δθ=0.6 Δθ(r_2 - r_1)\,\Delta\theta = 0.6\,\Delta\theta(r2​−r1​)Δθ=0.6Δθ.

  2. The ratio is 12(r22−r12)r2−r1=r1+r22\frac{\frac12 (r_2^2 - r_1^2)}{r_2 - r_1} = \frac{r_1 + r_2}{2}r2​−r1​21​(r22​−r12​)​=2r1​+r2​​, exactly the center radius. For polar coordinates the measured ratio and the central determinant agree by identity, not by luck.

Show the complex square map (u,v)↦(u2−v2,2uv)(u, v) \mapsto (u^2 - v^2, 2uv)(u,v)↦(u2−v2,2uv) has determinant 4(u2+v2)4(u^2 + v^2)4(u2+v2), and explain why a cell's measured area ratio is not exactly the center value here.

J=(2u−2v2v2u),det⁡J=4u2+4v2J = \begin{pmatrix} 2u & -2v \\ 2v & 2u \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \det J = 4u^2 + 4v^2J=(2u2v​−2v2u​),detJ=4u2+4v2
Show proof

  1. Collecting partials gives J=(2u−2v2v2u)J = \begin{pmatrix} 2u & -2v \\ 2v & 2u \end{pmatrix}J=(2u2v​−2v2u​) with determinant 4u2+4v2=4(u2+v2)4u^2 + 4v^2 = 4(u^2 + v^2)4u2+4v2=4(u2+v2).

  2. The measured ratio is close to the cell-wide average of the determinant, while the center value is a single point's value. When the determinant varies inside the cell, the two differ.

  3. Finer cells vary less, so the measured ratio converges to the center value. This is why the determinant appears in change of variables.
